label: token right after an x in the first or second original position (t = 1 or 2)
explanation: Fires during the original phase at t = 1 or t = 2 when the previous input was x, i.e. on the token right after an x at position 0 or 1. Nothing about the current token matters. On dev the predicate has precision 1.0 with no false positives, and it covers 99.97% of activation mass. Magnitude is highest when x is at position 0 and the feature fires at t = 1 (top examples sit near max, about 2.0). When x is at position 1 (the feature fires at t = 2) values are often lower (0.74-0.97 of max). It does not fire after an x at later positions (t >= 3, apart from a few weak cases such as x x p), and it never fires during the delimiter or copy phases. The missed activations are mostly near-zero (about 0.005) blips at t = 1 after a first token s, and they carry 0% of the mass.

issues: I could not refute the claims. On test the predicate scores precision 1.0, recall 0.964, F1 0.981 and mass recall 0.9997, with 0 false positives on either split.
Copy phase: it fires on 5 dev steps, so 'never fires in the copy phase' is very slightly overstated. Those 5 steps carry 0 activation mass and the delimiter step has 0 activations.
t=3 after an x: 132 dev activations, but the predicate (prev_tok==x)&(t==3) has precision 0.009 and mass 0.0003 on test. These are negligible blips, which fits the 'a few weak cases' wording.

The missed activations are one systematic group, not random noise: t=1 after a first token s, current token a or b (~1110 steps). They are about 0.005 of max and carry 0% of the mass, and the explanation already describes them. They are too small to be worth putting in the predicate.

Magnitude: (prev x)&(t==1) holds about 54% of the mass and all of the top quartile. The t=2 cases fall in lower quartiles (about 0.74-0.97 of max), as claimed. The current token may slightly change the size: the top examples all have b as the current token. It does not affect whether the feature fires.
